source: Somsak Wannasaree, "Banana Orchards" (Khmer translation, 1997), section 8 (pruning/thinning the clump)
text:
Rather than replanting a plot from scratch after each harvest, a banana clump can be kept continuously productive for many years by managing a staggered succession of suckers of different ages around the same base. This source recommends maintaining roughly four suckers of different ages at any one time within a clump: one at or near fruiting (the current "mother"), one about half-grown as the next replacement, one young follower, and one just-emerging start. As each mother stem finishes fruiting and is harvested, it is removed and the next-oldest sucker takes over as the new mother, while a new young sucker is allowed to start the cycle again at the base.

When selecting which sucker to keep at each thinning, farmers should also pay attention to its position around the clump: choosing suckers that emerge in a rotating position around the base (rather than clustering all replacements on one side) keeps the clump balanced and avoids overcrowding as it grows over successive generations.

One important timing detail: once a bunch has been harvested, the spent pseudostem should be cut down promptly, ideally within about 4-6 days, rather than left standing. A cut-down mother stem stops competing with the younger follow-on suckers for water and nutrients, which noticeably speeds their growth toward the next harvest.
